newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Typhoon Winnie kills 31 in Taiwan, 13 missing.
newsitem.headline: Typhoon Winnie kills 31 in Taiwan, 13 missing.

text.p: Typhoon Winnie killed at least 31 people in Taiwan on Monday and Tuesday and rescuers were searching for 13 people missing after a hillside security wall and 10 residential blocks collapsed.

Rescue teams working through the night found two more bodies in the rubble by Tuesday morning -- a son who died in the arms of his father -- and two other bodies in the afternoon, bringing to 15 the number of people killed by the collapse, police said.
Forty-eight people were injured, police added.
Typhoon Winnie hit northern Taiwan on Monday, triggering landslides and causing floods that turned streets into rivers.
A group of residents whose houses were flooded shouted their anger at Premier Lien Chan as he inspected an inundated residential area in Taipei.
"We want justice. Give us a safe living environment and we don't want to live in fear," said a teary-eyed woman whose relatives drowned in a basement.

They said shoddy construction materials and the government's failure to observe water and soil conservation, along with illegal property development on hillside land, were the causes of the landslides and floods.
Lien told the protesters the government "would find out who is to blame and to make remedies and rehabilitation."
Rescue authorities said they had sent more than 400 fire, military and police personnel to search for survivors in the collapsed blocks in the Taipei-area county of Hsichih.
But the rescue operation was slow and difficult because the first and second floors of the crumbled buildings were driven into the ground by the weight of the collapse.
The five-storey apartment complex gave way after a landslide toppled a security wall that crashed into the complex, police said.
"The whole scene looks as if it has gone through an explosion," a witness said.
Torrential rain from Typhoon Winnie swamped houses in low-lying areas of Taipei. Scores of cars and other vehicles were submerged on flooded roads.
The typhoon, packing maximum sustained winds of 144 km per hour (89 miles per hour) and gusts of up to 180 kph (112 mph), forced government offices, financial markets and schools to close on Monday.
Most had reopened on Tuesday, officials said.
The provincial government said Winnie inflicted T$202.34 million (US$7.22 million) worth of agricultural damage on Taiwan, according to preliminary estimates. (US$1 = T$28)
